definitions.definition: Rules in physics that say certain things (like energy or momentum) never change in total, no matter what happens.
definitions.example: Like a bank account where money can move between accounts but the total amount stays the same.

definitions.definition: Something that cannot be broken or disobeyed.
definitions.example: Like a rule that is absolutely impossible to break, no matter how hard you try.

definitions.definition: A property where something stays the same even when you change something about it, like rotating a perfect circle.
definitions.example: A snowflake looks the same when you rotate it 60 degrees.

definitions.definition: A famous math proof that every conservation law comes from a symmetry in nature.
definitions.example: Like discovering that if a game's rules don't change over time, the total score stays constant.

definitions.definition: The idea that the laws of physics work the same today as they did yesterday or will tomorrow.
definitions.example: Like gravity pulling an apple down the same way now as it did a thousand years ago.

definitions.definition: A basic assumption that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for other ideas.
definitions.example: Like saying 'all right angles are equal' in geometry—you just accept it to build other rules.

definitions.definition: A measurable thing, like energy or charge, that stays the same in a closed system over time.
definitions.example: Like the total number of marbles in a sealed box, no matter how you shake it.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; the Second Law says it always increases over time.
definitions.example: Like a messy bedroom that gets messier on its own unless you clean it up.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 'Why God Can't Look on Sin'

definitions.definition: The law of physics that says disorder (entropy) in a closed system always increases or stays the same.
definitions.example: Like ice melting into water—it spreads out and becomes more disordered naturally.
definitions.first_appearance: Section 'Why God Can't Look on Sin'

definitions.definition: A physics theory that says particles are really tiny ripples in invisible fields that fill all of space.
definitions.example: Like thinking of an electron as a little wave in an 'electron field' that exists everywhere.

definitions.definition: Something that carries a force or interaction between two things that cannot touch directly.
definitions.example: Like a messenger who delivers a letter between two people who never meet face to face.

definitions.definition: A tiny particle of light that carries the electromagnetic force between charged particles.
definitions.example: Like a tiny invisible ball that two magnets throw to each other to push or pull.

definitions.definition: A particle that holds quarks together inside protons and neutrons, like a tiny glue.
definitions.example: Like a super-strong rubber band that keeps three marbles stuck together.

definitions.definition: A hypothetical particle that would carry the force of gravity, if gravity works like other forces.
definitions.example: Like an invisible particle that Earth throws at the Moon to keep it in orbit.

definitions.definition: The Christian belief that God became a human being in the person of Jesus Christ.
definitions.example: Like a king becoming a peasant to live among his people and understand them.

definitions.definition: Negative entropy; a flow of order or information into a system, making it more organized.
definitions.example: Like adding fresh batteries to a toy to make it work again, bringing order back.

definitions.definition: Something that affects or connects things instantly across a distance, without traveling through space.
definitions.example: Like two magic coins that always show the same side, even if one is on Earth and the other on Mars.

definitions.definition: Kurt Gödel, a mathematician who proved that some true statements cannot be proven within a system.
definitions.example: Like a rulebook that can't prove its own rules are correct without looking outside the book.

definitions.definition: A term in this framework meaning the limit that God's saving power must be infinite to overcome entropy.
definitions.example: Like needing an infinite supply of clean water to purify an ocean of pollution.

definitions.definition: The process in quantum field theory where particles exchange force-carrying particles to interact.
definitions.example: Like two people playing catch with a ball to feel each other's push.
